name: tshark
one_line: dump and analyze network traffic (the command-line Wireshark)
plain: `tshark` is Wireshark without the windows. It reads network traffic live from a network card or from a capture file (.pcap, .pcapng) and prints what it finds, one line per packet or as precise extracted fields.

Its superpower is the display filter language, the same as in Wireshark: http.request.method == "POST", dns.qry.name contains "evil", tcp.port == 4444. With -T fields -e you pull exactly the values you want, which makes it ideal for scripts and quick CTF questions about a capture.
Two kinds of filter exist: a capture filter (-f) is the old tcpdump style and decides what is recorded; a display filter (-Y) decides what is shown from what was recorded. Beginners mix them up.
when: Answer questions about a .pcap: which IPs talk, what was requested, which credentials crossed in clear text.
Pull out specific fields, such as every DNS name or every HTTP URL.
Follow a TCP conversation and read it as text.
Export files carried inside HTTP or SMB.
Capture traffic on the lab network into a file for later.

examples.title: List the packets in a capture
examples.explain: -r reads a file. Each line shows packet number, time, source, destination, protocol and a short summary. Piping to head keeps the screen tidy.

examples.title: Show only HTTP requests
examples.explain: -Y is a display filter. Only packets that are HTTP requests are shown.

examples.title: Pull out exact fields
examples.cmd: tshark -r capture.pcap -Y http.request -T fields -e ip.src -e http.host -e http.request.uri
examples.explain: -T fields prints only the columns you ask for with -e. Result: who asked which host for which path, ready for sort and uniq.

examples.title: Every DNS name queried
examples.cmd: tshark -r capture.pcap -Y dns.flags.response==0 -T fields -e dns.qry.name | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
examples.explain: Filters DNS questions (not answers), extracts the names, then counts them. A strange name at the top is often malware or tunnelling.

examples.title: Follow a TCP conversation
examples.explain: -z follow,tcp,ascii,0 rebuilds stream number 0 as text, like Wireshark's 'Follow TCP Stream'. -q hides the packet list so only the conversation prints.

examples.title: Find clear-text credentials
examples.cmd: tshark -r capture.pcap -Y 'http.authbasic || ftp.request.command=="PASS"' -T fields -e ip.src -e http.authbasic -e ftp.request.arg
examples.explain: Basic auth and FTP passwords cross the wire in clear. This pulls them out.

examples.title: Statistics: who talks to whom
examples.explain: -z conv,ip prints a conversation table by IP pair with packet and byte counts. Good for finding the biggest talker.

examples.title: Export files from HTTP
examples.explain: Saves every file transferred over HTTP (images, scripts, downloads) into the folder ./out. Create it first.

examples.title: Capture live for 30 seconds
examples.explain: -i chooses the interface, -a duration:30 stops after 30 seconds, -w writes the raw capture to a file you can analyse later.

examples.title: Capture only one host, keep it small
examples.cmd: sudo tshark -i eth0 -f 'host 10.10.10.5 and port 80' -w web.pcap
examples.explain: -f is a capture filter in tcpdump syntax, applied before packets are stored, so the file stays small.

examples.title: Decrypt TLS with a key log
examples.explain: -o sets a preference. With the browser's SSLKEYLOGFILE data tshark can decrypt HTTPS and show the HTTP inside.

examples.title: Count packets per protocol
examples.explain: -z io,phs gives the 'protocol hierarchy statistics', a tree of how much traffic is HTTP, DNS, TLS and so on.

mistakes: Using -f where you meant -Y: -f is a capture filter and uses tcpdump syntax; -Y is a display filter with the Wireshark language.
Forgetting quotes around a display filter that contains spaces, || or &&; the shell eats them.
Running a live capture without sudo (or capture permissions): 'permission denied'.
Expecting HTTPS to be readable: you need the key log to decrypt it.
Writing a huge capture with no stop condition: use -a duration or -c.
